children: Saudi Arabia is considering storing crude oil and petroleum products in Egypt to ensure maximum export capacity during crises after its global oil supplies were hit by Iran’s closure of Hormuz Strait early this year.
The world’s largest oil exporter has been working round the clock to offset the decline by boosting export via pipelines bypassing the narrow strategic Straits.
The new plan is included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed by the oil ministers of Saudi Arabia and Egypt in Riyadh on Sunday.

Prince Abul Aziz bin Salman and his Egyptian counterpart Karim Badawi inked the deal “for enhancing cooperation between the two countries in the fields of petroleum, natural gas, and their derivatives,” Egypt’s petroleum and mineral resources ministry said.

“The MoU aims to expand cooperation and integration between the oil and energy sectors of both countries, maximizing the utilisation of available capabilities and expertise,” the ministry said on its website.

“This will be achieved by strengthening cooperation in the trade, handling, transportation, storage, and distribution of crude oil, petroleum products, and natural gas, as well as developing the infrastructure and logistics services associated with these activities…this will support the efficiency of energy markets and enhance the resilience and reliability of supply chains and energy security.”

Egypt has embarked on plans to expand its oil and gas storage facilities following the eruption of the US-Iran conflict in late February and the closure of Hormuz, which handles nearly 20 percent of the world’s seaborne oil trade.
(Writing by N Saeed; Editing by Anoop Menon)
